fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the thing that struck me most was how little we had to do. At the time, the way you got state-of-the-art on a language understanding task was to build an architecture for that task. Question answering had its own model, textual entailment had its own model, with attention mechanisms designed around the structure of the problem. And here we were taking a plain transformer decoder, training it to predict the next word on a corpus of books, and then fine-tuning it with basically a linear layer on top. That was it. No task-specific wiring, just a way of feeding the inputs in as a sequence with some delimiter tokens.

And it beat those carefully engineered systems on most of the benchmarks we tried. I remember feeling a little uneasy about it, because it almost felt like cheating. All this inductive bias that people had spent years designing turned out to be less useful than just reading a lot of text.

The other thing that stuck with me was the zero-shot behavior. We had a section in the paper where we looked at what the model could do with no fine-tuning at all, just by phrasing the task as text, and the performance kept going up the longer we pretrained. It wasn't good in absolute terms, but the trend was clean. That was the first hint for me that the language modeling objective was teaching the model something more general than word statistics. It was picking up on the tasks implicitly because people write about those tasks in books.

I don't think any of us saw how far that would scale. The transformer was only about a year old then, and it wasn't obvious it would be the right architecture for pure language modeling rather than translation. Alec had been doing earlier work with LSTMs, and the transformer just trained so much more cleanly on long contexts. In retrospect the recipe looks obvious, but at the time it felt like a surprisingly simple thing to work this well.

opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, what struck me most was how simple the recipe was relative to how well it worked. At the time, the dominant approach in NLP was to build a fairly specialized architecture for each task: one model for question answering, another for entailment, another for sentiment, each with its own bells and whistles. What we were doing was almost embarrassingly straightforward. Take a transformer decoder, train it on a large amount of unlabeled text with a plain next-word prediction objective, and then fine-tune that same model on a downstream task with very minimal changes, mostly just formatting the input the right way.

And it worked across the board. We saw improvements on a whole range of benchmarks, and on many of them we were beating models that had been carefully engineered for that specific task. That was the first surprise: a general-purpose pre-trained model could compete with, and often beat, task-specific designs.

The second thing, which I think in retrospect was the more important signal, came from the analysis we did on zero-shot behavior. Even before any fine-tuning, as pre-training went on, the model's ability to do certain tasks kept improving, even though it had never been explicitly trained on them. It was very rough at that scale, but it suggested that in learning to predict the next word, the model was picking up something more general about language and maybe about the world. That's the thread that later work pulled on very hard with scale.

There was also the architectural piece. Alec and others had already been exploring unsupervised language modeling with LSTMs, and there were hints there, like the sentiment neuron result. But moving to the transformer made a real difference. It handled longer-range context much better, and it trained much more efficiently on modern hardware. That combination of a scalable architecture with a scalable objective turned out to be the key.

To be honest, I don't think any of us fully anticipated where it would go. We thought of it as a strong transfer learning result. The idea that you'd keep scaling the same basic recipe and get the kind of capabilities we see today wasn't something I would have confidently predicted back then. But looking back, the seeds were there in that first paper.

fable-5.text:
Yeah, so this was back in 2017, 2018, and I think the thing that really struck me was how simple the recipe was and how surprisingly well it worked. The idea itself — pre-train a language model on a lot of unlabeled text and then fine-tune it on downstream tasks — wasn't completely new. People had tried versions of it with word embeddings, with LSTMs. But what we found was that when you combined the transformer architecture with just predicting the next word on a large corpus of books, the model picked up a remarkable amount about language, and even some reasoning, almost for free.

I remember being surprised at how broadly it transferred. We evaluated on something like twelve different tasks — natural language inference, question answering, semantic similarity, classification — and this single pre-trained model, with very minimal task-specific modification, was beating systems that had been carefully engineered for each individual task. That was the moment where it felt like something had shifted. You didn't need to build a bespoke architecture for every problem anymore; you could have one model that learned general-purpose representations and adapt it.

The other thing that stayed with me was the zero-shot behavior. Even without any fine-tuning, you could see the model doing non-trivial things on tasks it was never explicitly trained for, and those capabilities grew steadily as pre-training went on. At the time we treated that as an interesting side observation — it's a small section in the paper — but in hindsight it was really the seed of everything that came after with GPT-2 and GPT-3, this idea that scale plus generative pre-training gives you emergent capabilities. I don't think any of us fully appreciated just how far that trend would go, but the early signs were there, and that was genuinely exciting to see up close.

opus-5.text:
Two things, really, and they were connected.

The first was how little we had to do to the architecture. Coming out of my PhD, the standard practice in NLP was that every task got its own model — you'd design an architecture for entailment that was different from your architecture for question answering, with attention mechanisms hand-engineered for the structure of that problem. And what we found was that if you pre-trained one transformer on a lot of raw text, you could handle all of those tasks by just reformatting the input into a single sequence with a couple of delimiter tokens, throw a linear layer on top, and fine-tune. That felt almost like cheating. It suggested the task-specific scaffolding we'd all been building was substituting for knowledge the model could acquire on its own, given enough text.

The second thing — and this is the part I still think about — was the zero-shot curve. Alec had this habit of probing the model as it trained, before any fine-tuning, just using heuristics to read off answers from the language model directly. And that performance went up smoothly over the course of pre-training. That's a very different kind of evidence. It means the thing isn't just memorizing surface statistics that happen to be a useful initialization; it's accumulating something task-relevant as a byproduct of predicting the next word.

I'll say honestly: none of us sat in that room and said "this goes to a hundred billion parameters and writes code." But the direction of the gradient was unmistakable. Every time we gave it more text and more capacity, it got better, with no sign of the curve bending. In a field where everything plateaus, that was the striking thing.

What struck me most was how much simpler the recipe was than what we were used to. At the time, most NLP work meant a bespoke architecture for each task, whether that was entailment, question answering, or classification. Here we had one pretrained transformer, trained only to predict the next word on a pile of unlabeled text, and we could adapt it to very different tasks with only small changes. We mostly just reformatted the inputs into a sequence the model could read. A lot of that sequence was the same stuff it had seen in pretraining.

Looking back, it was a tiny model by today's standards, around a hundred million parameters, trained on a corpus of books. But it beat the task-specific systems on a lot of benchmarks. That told us the pretraining was teaching the model something general about language, and that it wasn't just a trick for one dataset.

The other thing that stuck with me was an analysis we did almost on the side. Even before any fine-tuning, the pretrained model could do some tasks to a small degree, and that ability kept improving as pretraining went on. It was a weak signal, but it suggested the language modeling objective itself was picking up useful skills. That thread, I think, is what led to everything that came after.

I'd also say that none of us thought of it as the start of something huge. It felt like a solid result and a promising direction. The scale of what followed was the real surprise.

That possibility—that language itself could provide such a useful training signal—was really compelling.
